arXiv:2301.06258v2 [math.AP] 30 Dec 2024

Attractors for the Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard System with Chemotaxis and Singular Potential in 2D

Jingning He Note: School of Mathematics, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou 311121, P.R. China. Email: hejingning@hznu.edu.cn
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We analyze the long-time behavior of solutions to a Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard system with chemotaxis effects and a solution-dependent mass source term. The fluid velocity 𝒗\bm{v} satisfies the Navier–Stokes system, the phase field variable φ\varphi satisfies a convective Cahn–Hilliard equation with a singular potential (e.g., the Flory–Huggins type), the nutrient density σ\sigma satisfies an advection-diffusion-reaction. For the initial boundary value problem in 2D, we prove the existence of the global attractor in a suitable phase space. Furthermore, we obtain the existence of an exponential attractor, and it can be implied that the global attractor is of finite fractal dimension.


Keywords: Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard system, Chemotaxis, Singular potential, Attractors.


MSC 2010: 35A01, 35A02, 35K35, 35Q92, 76D05.

1 Introduction

We investigate the following Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard type system

∂t𝒗+𝒗⋅∇𝒗−div(2η(φ)D𝒗)+∇p=(μ+χσ)∇φ,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{v}+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\bm{v}-\textrm{div}(2\eta(\varphi)D\bm{v})+\nabla p=(\mu+\chi\sigma)\nabla\varphi, (1.1a)
div​𝒗=0,\displaystyle\textrm{div}\ \bm{v}=0, (1.1b)
∂tφ+𝒗⋅∇φ=Δ​μ−M⁡(x,φ),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\varphi=\Delta\mu-M(x,\varphi), (1.1c)
μ=A​Ψ′​(φ)−B​Δ​φ−χ​σ,\displaystyle\mu=A\varPsi^{\prime}(\varphi)-B\Delta\varphi-\chi\sigma, (1.1d)
∂tσ+𝒗⋅∇σ=Δ⁡(σ+χ⁡(1−φ))+S,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\sigma=\Delta(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi))+S, (1.1e)

in Ω×(0,T)\Omega\times(0,T). Here, Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega and T>0T>0 is a given final time of arbitrary magnitude. The system is subject to the following boundary conditions

𝒗=𝟎,∂𝒏φ=∂𝒏μ=∂𝒏σ=0,\displaystyle\bm{v}=\mathbf{0},\quad{\partial}_{\bm{n}}\varphi={\partial}_{\bm{n}}\mu={\partial}_{\bm{n}}\sigma=0,\qquad\qquad on ∂Ω×(0,T),\displaystyle\ \partial\Omega\times(0,T), (1.2)

and the initial conditions

𝒗|t=0=𝒗0​(x),φ|t=0=φ0​(x),σ|t=0=σ0​(x),\displaystyle\bm{v}|_{t=0}=\bm{v}_{0}(x),\ \ \varphi|_{t=0}=\varphi_{0}(x),\ \ \sigma|_{t=0}=\sigma_{0}(x),\qquad in Ω.\displaystyle\ \Omega. (1.3)

Here, 𝒏=𝒏⁡(x)\bm{n}=\bm{n}(x) denotes the unit outward normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

System (1.1a)–(1.1e) can be regarded as a simplified version of the general thermodynamically consistent diffuse interface model in [31] where the authors study a two-component incompressible fluid mixture including a chemical species subject to diffusion and some significant transport mechanisms, like advection and chemotaxis (see also [39] and the references cited therein). In this system, the state variables of the system are volume-averaged velocity 𝒗\bm{v}, the (modified) pressure pp, the difference in volume fractions of the binary mixture φ\varphi, the concentration of the chemical species σ\sigma, the chemical potential μ\mu associated to (φ,σ)(\varphi,\sigma). Here, D​𝒗=12​(∇𝒗+(∇𝒗)T)D\bm{v}=\frac{1}{2}(\nabla\bm{v}+(\nabla\bm{v})^{\mathrm{T}}) denotes the symmetrized velocity gradient. The potential Ψ\varPsi denotes the physically relevant free energy density given by the logarithmic type [6]:

Ψ⁡(r)=θ2​[(1−r)​ln⁡(1−r)+(1+r)​ln⁡(1+r)]+θ02​(1−r2),∀r∈[−1,1],\varPsi(r)=\frac{\theta}{2}\big[(1-r)\ln(1-r)+(1+r)\ln(1+r)\big]+\frac{\theta_{0}}{2}(1-r^{2}),\quad\forall\,r\in[-1,1], (1.4)

with 0<θ<θ00<\theta<\theta_{0} (see, e.g., [6, 7]), which is also known as Flory–Huggins potential.

The source term M⁡(x,φ)M(x,\varphi) in (1.1c) (see (H4) below) is related to biological mechanisms like proliferation, elimination of cells (see e.g., [30]). Further discussions on biologically relevant mass source terms can be found in [33] and the references cited therein. The source term M⁡(x,φ)M(x,\varphi) can be viewed as a general form of Oono’s type α⁡(φ−c0)\alpha(\varphi-c_{0}) with α≥0\alpha\geq 0, c0∈(−1,1)c_{0}\in(-1,1), which represents nonlocal interactions (e.g. reversible chemical reaction) between the two components (cf. [21, 32]). Assuming that the components η1\eta_{1}, η2>0\eta_{2}>0 are viscosities of the two homogeneous fluids, the mean viscosity is modeled by the concentration dependent term η=η⁡(φ)\eta=\eta(\varphi), for instance, a typical form is the linear combination:

η⁡(φ)=η1​1+φ2+η2​1−φ2.\eta(\varphi)=\eta_{1}\frac{1+\varphi}{2}+\eta_{2}\frac{1-\varphi}{2}. (1.5)

The positive constant AA is the surface tension coefficient, and the positive coefficient BB is related to thickness of the interfacial layer (i.e., the diffuse interface). The constant χ\chi is related to certain specific transport mechanisms such as chemotaxis and active transport in the context of tumor growth modelling (see e.g., [18, 16]). As it has been shown in [27, 31], the following basic energy law holds for the problem (1.1a)–(1.3)

dd​t​∫Ω[12​|𝒗|2+A​Ψ​(φ)+B2​|∇φ|2+12​|σ|2+χ​σ​(1−φ)]​𝑑x\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}\Big[\frac{1}{2}|\bm{v}|^{2}+A\varPsi(\varphi)+\frac{B}{2}|\nabla\varphi|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}|\sigma|^{2}+\chi\sigma(1-\varphi)\Big]dx
+∫Ω[2η(φ)|D𝒗|2+m(φ)|∇μ|2+|∇(σ+χ(1−φ))|2]dx\displaystyle\qquad+\int_{\Omega}\Big[2\eta(\varphi)|D\bm{v}|^{2}+m(\varphi)|\nabla\mu|^{2}+|\nabla(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi))|^{2}\Big]dx
=∫Ω[−M⁡(x,φ)​μ+(−𝒞​h​(φ)​σ+S)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ))]​𝑑x,\displaystyle\quad=\int_{\Omega}\left[-M(x,\varphi)\mu+(-\mathcal{C}h(\varphi)\sigma+S)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi))\right]dx, (1.6)

which plays a significant role in the study of its global well-posedness.

The system (1.1a)–(1.3) with a regular potential was first investigated in [31]. The authors of [31] obtained the existence of global weak solutions in dimension two and three, the existence and uniqueness of global strong solutions in dimension two under an artificial assumption on the coefficients AA and χ\chi. This extra assumption was removed in the recent work [27], where the author considered a singular potential like (1.4) and proved the existence of global weak solutions in two and three dimensions. Then the authors in [28] proves the existence and regularity properties of the unique global strong solution for problem (1.1a)–(1.3) in two dimensions.

Neglecting the interaction due to nutrient and assuming α=0\alpha=0, our problem (1.1a)–(1.1d) reduces to the well-known “Model H” for two incompressible and viscous Newtonian fluids [29, 26]. This model has been extensively investigated in the literature under various hypotheses on mobility, fluid viscosity and potential function. For instance, for the Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard system, we refer to [5, 13, 43] for the regular potential case, and to [1, 5, 24] when the potential is singular (e.g., logarithmic). We refer to [4, 35] for the system with nonlocal effect due to Oono’s interaction. Concerning the long-time behavior of the NSCH system with regular potential, the existence of global and exponential attractors was proved in [13]. The lower bound for the global attractor can be found in [14], and the existence of a pullback exponential attractor was studied [3]. For the logarithmic potential case, we refer to [1] for the stability of local minima of the energy and the existence of the global attractor, and to the recent work [25] for the existence of the exponential attractor. Neglecting the fluid interaction in system (1.1a)–(1.1d), the well-posedness of a Cahn–Hilliard type system with chemotaxis was proved in [16], the case with Dirichlet boundary conditions was investigated in [15]. Neglecting chemotaxis and active transport effects, the existence of global attractors of some related diffuse interface models under a choice of the regular potential was proved in [12, 34]. Concerning the existence of exponential attractors for the Cahn–Hilliard equation, we refer to [36, 37] and the references therein.

Our aim is to continue the study of [27, 28] and establish the long-time behavior of problem (1.1a)–(1.3) with the choice of a singular potential like (1.4) in two dimensions from the viewpoint of infinite dimensional dynamical systems. Based on the well-posedness results in [27, 28] and the energy law (1.6) of the system, we define a semigroup map on a suitable phase-space. We prove the existence of a compact absorbing set in the phase-space and the strong continuity of the semigroup, which implies the existence of the global attractor (cf. [42]). Then, we obtain the existence of exponential attractors by showing the so-called smoothing property (cf. [38]). It is worth mentioning that the separation property (that is, φ\varphi stays away from the pure phases ±1\pm 1 from a certain time on) makes the Cahn–Hilliard equation with singular potential can be regarded as a parabolic equation with a globally Lipschitz potential. Finally, we prove some regularity properties of the global attractor and its finite fractal dimension.

The remaining part of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we state the functional settings and introduce the main results. In Section 3, we introduce the dynamical system related to problem (1.1a)–(1.1e) and prove the existence of the global attractor. Section 4 is devoted to the existence of an exponential attractor.

Remark 2.1.

The logarithmic potential (1.4) satisfies the assumptions (H2)\mathrm{(H2)} and (H3)\mathrm{(H3)}.

2.3 Statement of main results

For any given constants

m1∈[0,1),c0∈[−m1,m1],and​m2≥0,m_{1}\in[0,1),\quad c_{0}\in[-m_{1},m_{1}],\quad\text{and}\ m_{2}\geq 0,

we define the phase space

𝒳m1,m2={(𝒗,φ,σ)∈𝑳2(Ω)×H1(Ω)×L2(Ω):∥φ∥L∞≤1,|φ¯|≤m1,|σ¯|≤m2}\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}=\big\{(\bm{v},\varphi,\sigma)\in\bm{L}^{2}(\Omega)\times H^{1}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega)\,:\,\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq 1,\ |\overline{\varphi}|\leq m_{1},\ |\overline{\sigma}|\leq m_{2}\big\} (2.7)

endowed with the metric d⁡((𝒗1,φ1,σ1),(𝒗2,φ2,σ2))=‖𝒗1−𝒗2‖+‖φ1−φ2‖H1+‖σ1−σ2‖\mathrm{d}((\bm{v}_{1},\varphi_{1},\sigma_{1}),(\bm{v}_{2},\varphi_{2},\sigma_{2}))=\|\bm{v}_{1}-\bm{v}_{2}\|+\|\varphi_{1}-\varphi_{2}\|_{H^{1}}+\|\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2}\|. We can check easily that 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is a complete metric space.

We first prove the existence of a global attractor in 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}:

Theorem 2.3 (Global attractor).

Assume that the hypotheses (H1)–(H6) are satisfied. Problem (1.1c)–(1.3) generates a strongly continuous semigroup 𝒮⁡(t):𝒳m1,m2→𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{S}(t):\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}\to\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}} such that for all t≥0t\geq 0 it holds

𝒮⁡(t)​(𝒗0,φ0,σ0)=(𝒗⁡(t),φ⁡(t),σ⁡(t)),\mathcal{S}(t)(\bm{v}_{0},\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0})=(\bm{v}(t),\varphi(t),\sigma(t)),

where (𝐯,φ,σ)(\bm{v},\varphi,\sigma) is the unique global weak solution proved in Theorem 2.1 corresponding to the initial datum (𝐯0,φ0,σ0)∈𝒳m1,m2(\bm{v}_{0},\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0})\in\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}. Moreover, the dynamical system (𝒮⁡(t),𝒳m1,m2)(\mathcal{S}(t),\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}) has the connected global attractor 𝒜m1,m2⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}} such that
1. 𝒜m1,m2\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is a compact set in 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}};
2. 𝒜m1,m2\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is invariant in 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, i.e. S⁡(t)​𝒜m1,m2=𝒜m1,m2S(t)\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}}=\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, for every t≥0t\geq 0;
3. 𝒜m1,m2\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is an attracting set for S⁡(t)S(t) on 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, i.e. for every bounded set ℬ⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}},

limt→0dist𝑳2×H1×L2​(𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ,𝒜m1,m2)=0,∀t≥0,\lim_{t\to 0}\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}})=0,\quad\forall\,t\geq 0,

where dist𝐋2×H1×L2​(⋅,⋅,⋅)\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot) denotes the Hausdorff semidistance between two sets with respect to the metric of 𝐋2​(Ω)×H1​(Ω)×L2​(Ω)\bm{L}^{2}(\Omega)\times H^{1}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega).

Furthermore, we mention that 𝒜m1,m2\mathcal{A}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is bounded in 𝐇1​(Ω)×H3​(Ω)×H1​(Ω)\bm{H}^{1}(\Omega)\times H^{3}(\Omega)\times H^{1}(\Omega).

Next, we prove that the dynamical system (𝒮⁡(t),𝒳m1,m2)(\mathcal{S}(t),\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}) possesses an exponential attractor ℳm1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}}.

Theorem 2.4 (Exponential attractor).

Assume that the hypotheses (H1)–(H6) are satisfied. Moreover, we assume that Ψ\varPsi belongs to the class of functions C4​(−1,1)C^{4}(-1,1). The dynamical system (𝒮⁡(t),𝒳m1,m2)(\mathcal{S}(t),\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}) has an exponential attractor ℳm1,m2⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, which is bounded in 𝐇1​(Ω)×H3​(Ω)×H1​(Ω)\bm{H}^{1}(\Omega)\times H^{3}(\Omega)\times H^{1}(\Omega) and satisfies the following properties:

  • (1)\mathrm{(1)}

    ℳm1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is positively invariant in 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}} satisfying 𝒮⁡(t)​ℳm1,m2⊂ℳm1,m2\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}}\subset\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}} for all t≥0t\geq 0;

  • (2)\mathrm{(2)}

    ℳm1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}} has finite fractal dimension in 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}};

  • (3)\mathrm{(3)}

    ℳm1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}} is an exponentially attracting set, that is, there holds a constant ω>0\omega>0 such that, for every bounded set ℬ⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, there is a positive constant JJ satisfying

    dist𝑳2×H1×L2​(𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ,ℳm1,m2)≤J​e−ω​t,∀t≥0.\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{B},\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}})\leq Je^{-\omega t},\quad\forall\,t\geq 0.

3 Global attractor

We prove the existence of a global attractor for system (1.1c)–(1.3), that is, in a suitable phase space, the global attractor is a unique compact set which is invariant under the semigroup generated by the evolution system and is an absorbing set for any bounded set when time goes to infinity.

Before starting the proof, we obtain the following uniform estimates which not only hold in the two-dimensional case but also in the three-dimensional case.

Lemma 3.1.

Assume that the hypotheses (H1), (H2) and (H4)–(H6) are satisfied. The weak solution to problem (1.1a)–(1.3) exists on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty) and satisfies the following uniform-in-time estimates:

‖𝒗⁡(t)‖2+‖φ⁡(t)‖H12+‖σ⁡(t)‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{v}(t)\|^{2}+\|\varphi(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\sigma(t)\|^{2}
+∫tt+1(∥∇𝒗(s)∥2+∥φ(s)∥H24+∥∇μ(s)∥2+∥∇σ(s)∥2)ds≤C,∀t≥0,\displaystyle\quad+\int_{t}^{t+1}\big(\|\nabla\bm{v}(s)\|^{2}+\|\varphi(s)\|_{H^{2}}^{4}+\|\nabla\mu(s)\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma(s)\|^{2}\big)\,ds\leq C,\quad\forall\,t\geq 0, (3.1)
∫tt+1(‖∂tφ⁡(s)‖(H1)′2+‖∂tσ⁡(s)‖(H1)′2)​𝑑s≤C,∀t≥0,\displaystyle\int_{t}^{t+1}\big(\left\|\partial_{t}\varphi(s)\right\|_{(H^{1})^{\prime}}^{2}+\left\|\partial_{t}\sigma(s)\right\|_{(H^{1})^{\prime}}^{2}\big)\,ds\leq C,\quad\forall\,t\geq 0, (3.2)

where the constant CC depends on ‖𝐯0‖𝐇1\|\bm{v}_{0}\|_{\bm{H}^{1}}, ‖μ0‖H1\|\mu_{0}\|_{H^{1}}, ‖σ0‖H1\|\sigma_{0}\|_{H^{1}}, ‖φ0‖H1\|\varphi_{0}\|_{H^{1}}, ∫ΩΨ⁡(φ0)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}\varPsi(\varphi_{0})dx, coefficients of the system and Ω\Omega, but not on tt.

Proof. The existence of a global weak solution (𝒗,φ,μ,σ)(\bm{v},\varphi,\mu,\sigma) on an arbitrary time interval [0,T][0,T] can be obtained by applying a similar argument in the proof of [27, Theorems 2.1], where the author used a semi-Galerkin method such that the approximate solution satisfies

‖φ⁡(t)‖L∞≤1,t≥0.\|\varphi(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq 1,\quad t\geq 0. (3.3)

Thus, we only need to derive a priori estimates that are uniform in time, and we keep in mind that (3.3) holds in this process.

Integrating (1.1c) over Ω\Omega, we get

dd​t∫Ωφdx=−∫ΩM(x,φ)dx,\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\,dx=-\int_{\Omega}M(x,\varphi)\,dx, (3.4)

|φ¯​(t)|<1,∀t≥0.|\overline{\varphi}(t)|<1,\quad\forall\,t\geq 0. (3.5)

dd​t​∫Ωσ​𝑑x=∫ΩS⁡(x,t)​𝑑x,\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}\sigma dx=\int_{\Omega}S(x,t)\,dx,

σ¯​(t)=σ0¯+∫0tS⁡(s)¯​𝑑s,∀t≥0.\overline{\sigma}(t)=\overline{\sigma_{0}}+\int_{0}^{t}\overline{S(s)}ds,\quad\forall\,t\geq 0. (3.6)

Then it follows from the Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality that

‖σ‖≤CP​(‖∇σ‖+|σ¯|)≤CP​‖∇σ‖+C,\|\sigma\|\leq C_{P}(\|\nabla\sigma\|+|\overline{\sigma}|)\leq C_{P}\|\nabla\sigma\|+C, (3.7)

dd​tℰ(t)+𝒟(t)=−∫ΩM(x,φ)μdx+∫ΩS(σ+χ(1−φ))dx,\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}(t)+\mathcal{D}(t)=-\int_{\Omega}M(x,\varphi)\mu\,dx+\int_{\Omega}S(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi))\,dx, (3.8)

where

Proof of Theorem 2.4. The separation property (3.62) plays a significant role in the proof of the exponential attractor, as we can overcome the singularity at ±1\pm 1 of the derivatives of the potential Ψ\varPsi. We adapt the general framework in [10] (see also [11, 38]) and employ the abstract conclusions in [2, 19] to prove Theorem 2.4.

(𝒗,p,φ,μ,σ)=(𝒗1−𝒗2,p1−p2,φ1−φ2,μ1−μ2,σ1−σ2),\displaystyle(\bm{v},p,\varphi,\mu,\sigma)=(\bm{v}_{1}-\bm{v}_{2},p_{1}-p_{2},\varphi_{1}-\varphi_{2},\mu_{1}-\mu_{2},\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2}),

Then it holds

∂t𝒗+𝒗1⋅∇𝒗+𝒗⋅∇𝒗2−div​(2​η​(φ1)​D​𝒗)−div​(2​(η⁡(φ1)−η⁡(φ2))​D​𝒗2)+∇p\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{v}+\bm{v}_{1}\cdot\nabla\bm{v}+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\bm{v}_{2}-\textrm{div}(2\eta(\varphi_{1})D\bm{v})-\textrm{div}\big(2(\eta(\varphi_{1})-\eta(\varphi_{2}))D\bm{v}_{2}\big)+\nabla p
=(μ1+χσ1)∇φ+(μ+χσ)∇φ2,\displaystyle\quad=(\mu_{1}+\chi\sigma_{1})\nabla\varphi+(\mu+\chi\sigma)\nabla\varphi_{2}, (4.6a)
∂tφ+𝒗1⋅∇φ+𝒗⋅∇φ2=Δ​μ−a⁡(x)​(m⁡(φ1)−m⁡(φ2)),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi+\bm{v}_{1}\cdot\nabla\varphi+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\varphi_{2}=\Delta\mu-a(x)(m(\varphi_{1})-m(\varphi_{2})), (4.6b)
μ=A​Ψ′​(φ1)−A​Ψ′​(φ2)−B​Δ​φ−χ​σ,\displaystyle\mu=A\varPsi^{\prime}(\varphi_{1})-A\varPsi^{\prime}(\varphi_{2})-B\Delta\varphi-\chi\sigma, (4.6c)
∂tσ+𝒗1⋅∇σ+𝒗⋅∇σ2−Δ​σ=−χ​Δ​φ,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma+\bm{v}_{1}\cdot\nabla\sigma+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\sigma_{2}-\Delta\sigma=-\chi\Delta\varphi, (4.6d)

almost everywhere in Ω×(0,T)\Omega\times(0,T), and

𝒗=𝟎,∂𝒏φ=∂𝒏σ=∂𝒏μ=0,on∂Ω×(0,T),\displaystyle\bm{v}=\mathbf{0},\quad{\partial}_{\bm{n}}\varphi={\partial}_{\bm{n}}\sigma={\partial}_{\bm{n}}\mu=0,\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\ \textrm{on}\ \partial\Omega\times(0,T), (4.7a)
𝒗|t=0=𝟎,φ|t=0=0,σ|t=0=0,inΩ.\displaystyle\bm{v}|_{t=0}=\bm{0},\quad\varphi|_{t=0}=0,\quad\sigma|_{t=0}=0,\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\textrm{in}\ \Omega. (4.7b)

Multiplying (4.6a) by 𝒗\bm{v} and integrating over Ω\Omega, we find

12​dd​t​‖𝒗‖2+2​(η⁡(φ1)​D​𝒗,D​𝒗)=J1+J2+J3,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\bm{v}\|^{2}+2\big(\eta\left(\varphi_{1}\right)D\bm{v},D\bm{v}\big)=J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3}, (4.8)

where

J1\displaystyle J_{1} =−(𝒗1⋅∇𝒗,𝒗)−(𝒗⋅∇𝒗2,𝒗)=−(𝒗⋅∇𝒗2,𝒗),\displaystyle=-\left(\bm{v}_{1}\cdot\nabla\bm{v},\bm{v}\right)-\left(\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\bm{v}_{2},\bm{v}\right)=-\left(\bm{v}\cdot\nabla\bm{v}_{2},\bm{v}\right),
J2\displaystyle J_{2} =−2​((η⁡(φ1)−η⁡(φ2))​D​𝒗2,∇𝒗),\displaystyle=-2\left(\left(\eta\left(\varphi_{1}\right)-\eta\left(\varphi_{2}\right)\right)D\bm{v}_{2},\nabla\bm{v}\right),
J3\displaystyle J_{3} =((μ1+χσ1)∇φ,𝒗)+((μ+χσ)∇φ2,𝒗).\displaystyle=((\mu_{1}+\chi\sigma_{1})\nabla\varphi,\bm{v})+((\mu+\chi\sigma)\nabla\varphi_{2},\bm{v}).

From [28, Section 5], we have

‖𝒗1​(t)−𝒗2​(t)‖2+‖φ1​(t)−φ2​(t)‖H12+‖σ1​(t)−σ2​(t)‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{v}_{1}(t)-\bm{v}_{2}(t)\|^{2}+\|\varphi_{1}(t)-\varphi_{2}(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\sigma_{1}(t)-\sigma_{2}(t)\|^{2} (4.9)
+∫0t(∥𝒗1(s)−𝒗2(s)∥2𝑯1+∥φ1(s)−φ2(s)∥H32+∥σ1(s)−σ2(s)∥2H1)ds\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{t}\Big(\|\bm{v}_{1}(s)-\bm{v}_{2}(s)\|^{2}_{\bm{H}^{1}}+\|\varphi_{1}(s)-\varphi_{2}(s)\|_{H^{3}}^{2}+\|\sigma_{1}(s)-\sigma_{2}(s)\|^{2}_{H^{1}}\Big)\,ds
≤C1′(∥𝒗0,1−𝒗0,2∥2+∥φ0,1−φ0,2∥H12+∥σ0,1−σ0,2∥2),∀t∈[0,T].\displaystyle\leq C_{1}^{\prime}\Big(\|\bm{v}_{0,1}-\bm{v}_{0,2}\|^{2}+\|\varphi_{0,1}-\varphi_{0,2}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\sigma_{0,1}-\sigma_{0,2}\|^{2}\Big),\quad\forall\,t\in[0,T].

Then we prove the smoothing estimate for the difference of solutions. Multiplying (4.6a) by 𝑺​𝒗\bm{S}\bm{v} and integrating over Ω\Omega, we obtain

12​dd​t​‖∇𝒗‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2} =∫Ωdiv(2η(φ)D𝒗)⋅𝑺𝒗dx−∫Ω(𝒗1⋅∇)𝒗⋅𝑺𝒗dx−∫Ω(𝒗⋅∇)𝒗2⋅𝑺𝒗dx\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\textrm{div}(2\eta(\varphi)D\bm{v})\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx-\int_{\Omega}\left(\bm{v}_{1}\cdot\nabla\right)\bm{v}\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx-\int_{\Omega}(\bm{v}\cdot\nabla)\bm{v}_{2}\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx (4.10)
+∫Ω2div((η(φ1)−η(φ2))D𝒗2)⋅𝑺𝒗dx+∫Ω(μ1+χσ1)∇φ⋅𝑺𝒗dx\displaystyle+\int_{\Omega}2\operatorname{div}\left(\left(\eta\left(\varphi_{1}\right)-\eta\left(\varphi_{2}\right)\right)D\bm{v}_{2}\right)\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx+\int_{\Omega}(\mu_{1}+\chi\sigma_{1})\nabla\varphi\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx

By Lemma 2.1 for the Stokes operator 𝑺\bm{S}, there exists p∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))p\in L^{2}\left(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)\right) satisfying −Δ​𝒗+∇p=𝑺​𝒗-\Delta\bm{v}+\nabla p=\bm{S}\bm{v} and

‖p‖≤C​‖∇𝒗‖12​‖𝑺​𝒗‖12,‖p‖H1≤C​‖𝑺​𝒗‖.\|p\|\leq C\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\bm{S}\bm{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}},\quad\|p\|_{H^{1}}\leq C\|\bm{S}\bm{v}\|. (4.11)

∫Ωdiv​(2​η​(φ)​D​𝒗)⋅𝑺​𝒗​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\textrm{div}(2\eta(\varphi)D\bm{v})\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx
=∫Ωη(φ)Δ𝒗⋅𝑺𝒗dx+∫Ω2η′(φ1)(D𝒗∇φ1)⋅𝑺𝒗dx\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\eta(\varphi)\Delta\bm{v}\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx+\int_{\Omega}2\eta^{\prime}\left(\varphi_{1}\right)\left(D\bm{v}\nabla\varphi_{1}\right)\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx
=−∫Ωη(φ)|𝑺𝒗|2dx+∫Ωη(φ)∇p⋅𝑺𝒗dx+∫Ω2η′(φ1)(D𝒗∇φ1)⋅𝑺𝒗dx\displaystyle=-\int_{\Omega}\eta(\varphi)|\bm{S}\bm{v}|^{2}d\,x+\int_{\Omega}\eta(\varphi)\nabla p\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx+\int_{\Omega}2\eta^{\prime}\left(\varphi_{1}\right)\left(D\bm{v}\nabla\varphi_{1}\right)\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx
=−∫Ωη(φ)|𝑺𝒗|2dx−∫Ωη′(φ)p∇φ⋅𝑺𝒗dx+∫Ω2η′(φ1)(D𝒗∇φ1)⋅𝑺𝒗dx.\displaystyle=-\int_{\Omega}\eta(\varphi)|\bm{S}\bm{v}|^{2}\,dx-\int_{\Omega}\eta^{\prime}(\varphi)p\nabla\varphi\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx+\int_{\Omega}2\eta^{\prime}\left(\varphi_{1}\right)\left(D\bm{v}\nabla\varphi_{1}\right)\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx.

≤C​‖∇𝒗‖12​‖𝑺​𝒗‖32\displaystyle\leq C\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\bm{S}\bm{v}\|^{\frac{3}{2}}

≤C​‖∇𝒗‖12​‖𝑺​𝒗‖32\displaystyle\leq C\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\bm{S}\bm{v}\|^{\frac{3}{2}}

+∣∫Ω2(η′(φ1)D𝒗2∇φ+(η′(φ1)−η′(φ2))D𝒗2∇φ2)⋅𝑺𝒗dx∣\displaystyle+\mid\int_{\Omega}2(\eta^{\prime}(\varphi_{1})D\bm{v}_{2}\nabla\varphi+(\eta^{\prime}(\varphi_{1})-\eta^{\prime}(\varphi_{2}))D\bm{v}_{2}\nabla\varphi_{2})\cdot\bm{S}\bm{v}\,dx\mid

≤B8​‖Δ2​φ‖2+C11′​‖∇𝒗‖2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{B}{8}\left\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\right\|^{2}+C_{11}^{\prime}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}.

Recalling (H3), we notice that

−∫Ω(a(x)(m(φ1)−a(x)(m(φ2))Δ2φdx\displaystyle-\int_{\Omega}(a(x)(m(\varphi_{1})-a(x)(m(\varphi_{2}))\Delta^{2}\varphi\,dx ≤∥a(x)(m(φ1)−a(x)(m(φ2)∥∥Δ2φ∥\displaystyle\leq\|a(x)(m(\varphi_{1})-a(x)(m(\varphi_{2})\|\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\|
≤B8​‖Δ2​φ‖2+C​‖φ‖2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{B}{8}\left\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\right\|^{2}+C\|\varphi\|^{2}. (4.17)

We deduce from Young’s inequality that

−∫ΩχΔσΔ2φdx≤B8∥Δ2φ∥+4​χ2B∥Δσ∥2.-\int_{\Omega}\chi\Delta\sigma\Delta^{2}\varphi\,dx\leq\frac{B}{8}\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\|+\frac{4\chi^{2}}{B}\|\Delta\sigma\|^{2}. (4.18)

From the above estimates together, we obtain

dd​t​(12​‖∇𝒗‖2+12​‖Δ​φ‖2)+B2​‖Δ2​φ‖2\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}\right)+\frac{B}{2}\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\|^{2} (4.19)
≤C12′​(1+‖𝐒​𝒗2‖2)​(12​‖∇𝒗‖2+12​‖Δ​φ‖2)+4​χ2B​‖Δ​σ‖2.\displaystyle\leq C_{12}^{\prime}\left(1+\left\|\mathbf{S}\bm{v}_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}\right)+\frac{4\chi^{2}}{B}\|\Delta\sigma\|^{2}.

Multiplying (4.6d) by −Δ​σ-\Delta\sigma and integrating over Ω\Omega, we obtain

12​dd​t​‖∇σ‖2+‖Δ​σ‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}+\|\Delta\sigma\|^{2} =χ​∫ΩΔ​φ​Δ​σ​𝑑x\displaystyle=\chi\int_{\Omega}\Delta\varphi\Delta\sigma\,dx (4.20)
≤12​‖Δ​σ‖2+χ22​‖Δ​φ‖2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\|\Delta\sigma\|^{2}+\frac{\chi^{2}}{2}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}.

Multiplying (4.20) by B16​χ2\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}} (as the decoupling case χ=0\chi=0 is indeed easier, we only need to consider χ≠0\chi\neq 0), adding (4.19) and (4.20) together, we obtain

12​dd​t​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2)+B232​χ2​‖Δ2​φ‖2+14​‖Δ​σ‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\Big(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\Big)+\frac{B^{2}}{32\chi^{2}}\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\|\Delta\sigma\|^{2}
≤C13′​(1+‖𝑺​𝒗2‖2)​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2).\displaystyle\quad\leq C_{13}^{\prime}\left(1+\left\|\bm{S}\bm{v}_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)\left(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\right). (4.21)

As a consequence, we infer that

12​dd​t​t​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2)+t⁡(B232​χ2​‖Δ2​φ‖2+14​‖Δ​σ‖2)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}t\Big(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\Big)+t(\frac{B^{2}}{32\chi^{2}}\|\Delta^{2}\varphi\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\|\Delta\sigma\|^{2}) (4.22)
≤C14′​t​(1+‖𝑺​𝒗2‖2)​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2)\displaystyle\leq C_{14}^{\prime}t\left(1+\left\|\bm{S}\bm{v}_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)\left(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\right)
+12​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2).\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\Big).

It can be implied from the Gronwall lemma that

t2​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2)\displaystyle\frac{t}{2}\Big(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\Big) (4.23)
≤C15′​∫0t(s+1)​(B16​χ2​‖∇𝒗‖2+B16​χ2​‖Δ​φ‖2+‖∇σ‖2)​𝑑s,\displaystyle\leq C_{15}^{\prime}\int_{0}^{t}(s+1)\Big(\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\nabla\bm{v}\|^{2}+\frac{B}{16\chi^{2}}\|\Delta\varphi\|^{2}+\|\nabla\sigma\|^{2}\Big)\,ds,

From (4.9) and (4.23), we prove the smoothing estimate:

‖𝒗1​(t)−𝒗2​(t)‖𝑯1+‖φ1​(t)−φ2​(t)‖H2+‖σ1​(t)−σ2​(t)‖H1\displaystyle\|\bm{v}_{1}(t)-\bm{v}_{2}(t)\|_{\bm{H}^{1}}+\|\varphi_{1}(t)-\varphi_{2}(t)\|_{H^{2}}+\|\sigma_{1}(t)-\sigma_{2}(t)\|_{H^{1}} (4.24)
≤CT​(1+tt)​(‖𝒗01−𝒗02‖+‖φ01−φ02‖H1+‖σ01−σ02‖),\displaystyle\leq C_{T}\left(\frac{1+t}{t}\right)(\|\bm{v}_{01}-\bm{v}_{02}\|+\|\varphi_{01}-\varphi_{02}\|_{H^{1}}+\|\sigma_{01}-\sigma_{02}\|),

for any t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T]. Here, the positive constant CTC_{T} depends on the constants R1>0R_{1}>0, coefficients of the system, R0R_{0}, Ω\Omega and TT. For any t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], there exists a constant C∗C^{*} depending on the coefficients of the system, norms of the initial data, Ω\Omega, TT and tt such that

‖S⁡(t)​(𝒗01,φ01,σ01)−S⁡(t)​(𝒗02,φ02,σ02)‖𝑯1​(Ω)×H2​(Ω)×H1​(Ω)\displaystyle\left\|S\left(t\right)\left(\bm{v}_{01},\varphi_{01},\sigma_{01}\right)-S\left(t\right)\left(\bm{v}_{02},\varphi_{02},\sigma_{02}\right)\right\|_{\bm{H}^{1}(\Omega)\times H^{2}(\Omega)\times H^{1}(\Omega)} (4.25)
≤C∗​‖(𝒗01,φ01,σ01)−(𝒗02,φ02,σ02)‖𝒳m1,m2.\displaystyle\leq C^{*}\left\|\left(\bm{v}_{01},\varphi_{01},\sigma_{01}\right)-\left(\bm{v}_{02},\varphi_{02},\sigma_{02}\right)\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}}.

The proof is complete. ∎

Step 3. Employing the abstract result [2, Lemma 5.3] (we cite to [19, Section 2] for the more general version), we can imply from Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 that there exists a closed bounded set ℳm1,m2⊂ℬ~1\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}}\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}, which is of finite fractal dimension in 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}} and positively invariant under 𝒮⁡(t)\mathcal{S}(t). Furthermore, there exist constants ω0>0\omega_{0}>0 and J0>0J_{0}>0 such that

dist𝑳2×H1×L2​(𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ~1,ℳm1,m2)≤J0​e−ω0​t,∀t≥0.\displaystyle\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\mathcal{S}(t)\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1},\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}})\leq J_{0}e^{-\omega_{0}t},\quad\forall\,t\geq 0.

For every bounded set ℬ⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, there exists t2=t2​(ℬ)>0t_{2}=t_{2}(\mathcal{B})>0 satisfying 𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ⊂ℬ~1\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{B}\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1} for all t≥t2​(ℬ)t\geq t_{2}(\mathcal{B}) (notice that ℬ~1\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1} itself is a compact absorbing set). Thus,

dist𝑳2×H1×L2​(𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ,ℳm1,m2)≤J0​e−ω0​[t−t2​(ℬ)],∀t≥t2​(ℬ).\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{B},\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}})\leq J_{0}e^{-\omega_{0}[t-t_{2}(\mathcal{B})]},\quad\forall\,t\geq t_{2}(\mathcal{B}).

It can be deduced from the above estimates and the boundedness of ℳm1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}} that

dist𝑳2×H1×L2​(𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ,ℳm1,m2)\displaystyle\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{B},\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}})
≤sup(𝒗,φ,σ)∈ℬsupt∈[0,t2​(ℬ)]‖𝒮⁡(t)​(𝒗,φ,σ)‖𝑳2×H1×L2+sup(𝒗,φ,σ)∈ℳm1,m2‖(𝒗,φ,σ)‖𝑳2×H1×L2\displaystyle\quad\leq\sup_{(\bm{v},\varphi,\sigma)\in\mathcal{B}}\sup_{t\in[0,\,t_{2}(\mathcal{B})]}\|\mathcal{S}(t)(\bm{v},\varphi,\sigma)\|_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}+\sup_{(\bm{v},\varphi,\sigma)\in\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}}}\|(\bm{v},\varphi,\sigma)\|_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}
≤Cℬ,∀t∈[0,t2​(ℬ)).\displaystyle\quad\leq C_{\mathcal{B}},\quad\forall\,t\in[0,t_{2}(\mathcal{B})).

Here, the constant Cℬ>0C_{\mathcal{B}}>0 depends on the size of ℬ\mathcal{B}, R1R_{1}, Ω\Omega, m1m_{1}, m2m_{2} and coefficients of the system. As a consequence, for every bounded set ℬ⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, it holds

dist𝑳2×H1×L2​(𝒮⁡(t)​ℬ,ℳm1,m2)≤(max⁡{J0,Cℬ}​eω0​t2​(ℬ))​e−ω0​t,∀t≥0.\displaystyle\mathrm{dist}_{\bm{L}^{2}\times H^{1}\times L^{2}}(\mathcal{S}(t)\mathcal{B},\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}})\leq\big(\max\{J_{0},C_{\mathcal{B}}\}e^{\omega_{0}t_{2}(\mathcal{B})}\big)e^{-\omega_{0}t},\quad\forall\,t\geq 0.

This implies that ℳm1,m2\mathcal{M}_{m_{1},m_{2}} attracts exponentially fast all bounded subsets ℬ⊂𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}, that is, its basin of exponential attraction is the whole phase space 𝒳m1,m2\mathcal{X}_{m_{1},m_{2}}.

The proof of Theorem 2.4 is complete. □\square
